knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 9,
  fig.height = 6, dpi = 220)

# Load the example

Compare human full-length AS3MT, a **paper-defined d2d3 reconstruction**,
and chimpanzee full-length AS3MT. Coordinates use **GRCh38** and
**Pan_tro_3.0**, respectively. All inputs are bundled; no downloads are needed.

```{r as3mt-load, message=FALSE}
library(ggexon)
library(ggplot2)
demo_dir <- system.file("extdata", "as3mt", package = "ggexon")
source(file.path(demo_dir, "load-as3mt-example.R"), local = TRUE)
as3mt <- load_as3mt_example(demo_dir)
```

# 1. Transcripts and compressed introns

`geom_exon2()` shows CDS as thick boxes and UTR as thin boxes. Keep the
full-reference exon numbering: d2d3 retains **E1 and E4–E11**; dashed boxes
mark skipped E2/E3. `scale_x_ggexon_genomic(intron_factor = 30)` compresses
introns 30-fold while keeping exon widths. `geom_nuclink()` automatically
follows that same piecewise scale in both annotation panels.

```{r as3mt-pairwise, fig.alt="Human full-length and paper-defined d2d3 transcript rows above the chimpanzee reference. Gold E2/E3 are skipped in d2d3; ribbons follow 30-fold intron compression.", fig.cap="Transcript comparison; introns compressed 30-fold."}
as3mt_plot <- plot_as3mt_example(as3mt, intron_factor = 30, show_protein = FALSE)
as3mt_plot$plot
```

The helper uses this grammar:

```{r as3mt-core-grammar, eval=FALSE}
ggexon(as3mt$comparison) +
  geom_exon2(aes(xmin = xmin - 0.5, xmax = xmax + 0.5,
    ymin = isoform_y, transcripts = transcript_name, fill = exon_class),
    annotation_type = "all", compress_introns = FALSE,
    utr_height = 0.35, cds_height = 1) +
  geom_nuclink(alignment = "human_chimp", aes(fill = identity_band),
    inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_genomics(vars(track), scales = "free_x", ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_ggexon_genomic(intron_factor = 30,
    guide = guide_x_ggexon_piecewise(by = "panel"))
```

Ribbons retain the two highest LASTZ identity categories, **97.1–98.3%** and
**98.3–100%**. The 37 ungapped blocks split into 57 polygon pieces at scale
boundaries. They show DNA similarity, not expression or proof of exon skipping.

# 2. Protein change on the human reference

The assigned d2d3 protein contains **273 aa**, corresponding to canonical
human residues **103–375** instead of 1–375. Its loss of **102 N-terminal aa**
is a consequence of the assigned downstream start; E2/E3 skipping removes
169 RNA bases, not a 306-nt in-frame deletion.

Project residue 103 through the **full-length human CDS** with
`project_mutations_to_genome()`. Its codon is **GRCh38 chr10:102872584–102872586**
in E4. The example helper returns that projection:

```{r as3mt-protein-change}
protein_change <- as3mt_protein_change(as3mt)
knitr::kable(protein_change[, c("position", "xmin", "xmax", "lost_aa")],
  col.names = c("Canonical residue", "Codon start", "Codon end", "Lost aa"))
```

Show the protein consequence with two distinct annotations:

- An orange interval marks canonical **aa1–102 absent from d2d3**. It is
  projected through the full-length CDS and split across coding exons; introns
  are not highlighted. This is a protein loss, not a 306-bp genomic deletion.
- A vertical start tick marks **M103**, which becomes **M1 in d2d3**. Both
  residues are methionine; there is no amino-acid substitution at this site.

```{r as3mt-protein-grammar, eval=FALSE}
protein_loss <- as3mt_protein_loss(as3mt)
as3mt_plot$plot + as3mt_protein_layers(protein_change, protein_loss)
```

The helpers use `project_domains_to_genome()` for the absent protein interval,
then `geom_rect()`, `geom_segment()` and `geom_text()` for its display. All
layers stay on the human reference panel and follow the genomic scale.
Substitution lollipops are reserved for actual reference/alternative residues.

# 3. DNA detail at the exon-1 repeat

The selected human reference contains three **36-bp VNTR** units; the chimp
reference has one imperfect homolog (34/36 matching bases). The terminal unit
contains 24 exonic and 12 intronic bases. Both references retain the **GT** donor:

```text
CCTGAGTCGCAGGCCGAGGAGACA | GTGAGTGCGCGC
         human exon 1  | intron 1
```

Prepare two aligned strings with an explicitly named human reference.
`-` denotes a gap and does not consume genomic bases. The strings are verified
against the bundled FASTAs; the donor-anchored alignment places 72 chimp gap
columns opposite two human repeat copies.

```{r as3mt-sequence-data}
v <- readRDS(file.path(demo_dir, "vntr-dna.rds"))
sequence_data <- alignseq_data(v$aligned, v$anchors, reference = "human",
  regions = v$regions, details = v$details, flank = 0)
```

`geom_alignseq()` places each species' DNA on its own panel. Default markers
show differences, with DNA callouts for selected details. Letters are equally
spaced schematically; smooth connectors retain genomic anchors. For a short
window, `mode = "rows"` shows all selected bases:

```{r as3mt-alignseq-rows, fig.height=3.75, fig.alt="Human and chimp terminal repeat DNA on separate annotation panels. The donor divides 24 exonic from 12 intronic bases."}
sequence_example <- plot_as3mt_alignseq(demo_dir, intron_factor = 30)
sequence_example$rows
```

Cai et al. tested otherwise matched **two- and three-repeat human minigenes**;
three repeats produced more d2d3. This supports repeat-dependent splicing
regulation, but does not establish sufficiency for the isoform's evolutionary
origin. The human allele experiment differs by **36 bp**; the figure's **−72 bp**
marker instead compares the selected chimp and human references. Two base
differences in the chimp homolog are context, not demonstrated causal SNVs.

# Sources and reproducibility

- [Li et al. (2016), doi:10.1038/nm.4096](https://doi.org/10.1038/nm.4096):
  d2d3 reconstruction, protein assignment and repeat sequence.
- [Cai et al. (2021), doi:10.1093/schbul/sbaa098](https://doi.org/10.1093/schbul/sbaa098):
  human VNTR minigene comparison.

The installed `extdata/as3mt` directory contains the plotting helper, input
snapshots and provenance. Repository preparation/export scripts are in
`data-raw/as3mt`; the genomic ribbons use LASTZ `--nogapped --chain` blocks.

# Combined result

The human reference shows **aa1–102 absent** and a **start tick at M103 (d2d3 M1)**.
Purple outlines locate
the VNTR; each species keeps its own DNA callout. Separate bars below the legend
show exon and compressed-intron scales. The lower human transcript remains a
**paper-defined reconstruction**; the repeat-count strip summarizes the tested
human alleles schematically.

```{r as3mt-alignseq, fig.height=6.5, fig.alt="Combined AS3MT transcript comparison with an orange interval split across human coding exons for canonical residues 1–102 absent from d2d3, and a separate E4 start tick labelled M103 to M1. Purple VNTR units, species-specific DNA callouts, and separate exon/intron scale bars complete the figure.", fig.cap="AS3MT transcripts, assigned protein-start change and exon-1 VNTR."}
grid::grid.newpage()
grid::grid.draw(sequence_example$grob)
```
